title: Fixed-width Boolean satisfiability

problem.name: $k$-SAT
problem.statement_latex:
Fix an integer $k\ge3$. Given
\[
 F(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\bigwedge_{j=1}^{m}C_j,
 \qquad |C_j|\le k,
\]
where each $C_j$ is a disjunction of literals, output $x\in\{0,1\}^n$ satisfying $F(x)=1$, or decide that none exists. The clause list is supplied explicitly. SAT represents Boolean feasibility in constraint programming and exact optimization.
The comparison uses quantum gate complexity and classical bit complexity on explicit formula inputs.
problem.statement_text: Fix an integer $k\ge3$. Given \[ F(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\bigwedge_{j=1}^{m}C_j, \qquad |C_j|\le k, \] where each $C_j$ is a disjunction of literals, output $x\in\{0,1\}^n$ satisfying $F(x)=1$, or decide that none exists. The clause list is supplied explicitly. SAT represents Boolean feasibility in constraint programming and exact optimization. The comparison uses quantum gate complexity and classical bit complexity on explicit formula inputs.

quantum.details_latex: These are bounded-error trial-amplification bounds, with polynomial factors for formula evaluation suppressed. They assume coherent evaluation and reversal of the classical randomized trial. Running the classical counting algorithm below on a quantum computer also supplies a subexponential upper bound for explicit $k$-SAT.

They assume coherent evaluation and reversal of the classical randomized trial. Running the classical counting algorithm below on a quantum computer also supplies a subexponential upper bound for explicit $k$-SAT.

classical.headline_latex: $(n+m)^{O_k(1)}2^{O_k(n\log\log n/\sqrt{\log n})}$, exact counting by Boolean tensor contraction.
classical.headline_text: $(n+m)^{O_k(1)}2^{O_k(n\log\log n/\sqrt{\log n})}$, exact counting by Boolean tensor contraction.
classical.details_latex:
The algorithm is deterministic and uses polynomial space. For $m\le Dn$ with fixed $D$, the time is
$(n+m)^{O_{k,D}(1)}2^{O_{k,D}(n/\sqrt{\log n})}$.
Positivity of the count decides satisfiability; conditional counts recover an assignment with polynomial overhead.

strength.description_latex: The subexponential classical bound is asymptotically smaller than the displayed amplified-trial bounds. Its exponent is $n^{1-o(1)}$, so the reduction from exponential to subexponential time has no power saving.
strength.description_text: The subexponential classical bound is asymptotically smaller than the displayed amplified-trial bounds. Its exponent is $n^{1-o(1)}$, so the reduction from exponential to subexponential time has no power saving.

evidence.description_latex: The stated algorithms have rigorous upper bounds. The comparison supplies no asymptotic quantum-speedup claim for amplified Sch\"oning or PPSZ.
evidence.description_text: The stated algorithms have rigorous upper bounds. The comparison supplies no asymptotic quantum-speedup claim for amplified Schöning or PPSZ.

hardware.description_latex:
The amplified-trial constructions require fault tolerance, $n$ assignment qubits, polynomial reversible workspace and exponentially many coherent trial evaluations.

{\small [Before ``ETH is false'', the known general classical 3-SAT bound was $O^*(1.30704^n)$, and amplified PPSZ claimed a quadratic improvement to $O^*(1.1433^n)$.]\par}
